stem:
Calculate i) total resistance and ii) total current in the following circuit.
\(R_{1} = 3\ \Omega\), \(R_{2} = 6\ \Omega\), \(R_{3} = 5\ \Omega\), \(V = 14\) V
solution:
i) Total resistance \(= R_{T} = R_{P} + R_{3}\)
\(R_{P} = \dfrac{R_{1}R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}} = \dfrac{3 \times 6}{9} = 2\ \Omega\)
\(R_{T} = 2 + 5 = 7\ \Omega\)
Total Resistance \(= 7\ \Omega\)
ii) Total current :
\(I = \dfrac{V}{R_{T}} = \dfrac{14\ \text{V}}{7\ \Omega}\)
\(I = 2\) A

stem: Calculate the resistance per metre, at room temperature, of a constantan (alloy) wire of diameter 1.25 mm. The resistivity of constantan at room temperature is \(5.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \Omega\)m.
solution:
\(\rho = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \Omega\)m
\(d = 1.25 \times 10^{-3}\) m
\(r = 0.625 \times 10^{-3}\) m
Cross-sectional Area \(= \pi r^{2}\)
Resistivity \(\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l}\)
Resistance per meter \(= \dfrac{R}{l}\)
i.e. \(\dfrac{R}{l} = \dfrac{\rho}{A} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-7}}{(0.625 \times 10^{-3})^{2} \times 3.142}\)
\(\dfrac{R}{l} = 0.41\ \Omega m^{-1}\)
\(\therefore\) Resistance per metre \(= 0.41\ \Omega\)m\(^{-1}\)

stem: A piece of platinum wire has resistance of \(2.5\ \Omega\) at \(0^{\circ}\)C. If its temperature coefficient of resistance is \(4 \times 10^{-3}/^{\circ}\)C. Find the resistance of the wire at \(80^{\circ}\)C.

A network of resistors is connected to a 15 V battery with internal resistance \(1\ \Omega\) as shown in the circuit diagram.
Calculate
(i) The equivalent resistance,
(ii) Current in each resistor,
(iii) Voltage drops \(V_{AB}\), \(V_{BC}\) and \(V_{DC}\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed line for \(V_{BC}\) is wrong three ways at once — it states the relation as \(I \times 1\), then substitutes \(2.1 \times 2.1\), and prints a result of \(2\) V that matches NEITHER reading (\(2.1 \times 2.1 = 4.41\); \(2.1 \times 1 = 2.1\)). The correct value is \(2.1\) V, which is what this example's OWN closing Note uses. Separately, the stem asks for \(V_{AB}\), \(V_{BC}\) and \(V_{DC}\), but the printed working never derives \(V_{AB}\) — while the same Note quotes \(4.2\) V for it. The derivation above has been corrected and the missing \(V_{AB} = I \times R_{AB} = 2.1 \times 2 = 4.2\) V supplied.]

i) Equivalent Resistance \((R_{eq}) = R_{AB} + R_{BC} + R_{DC}\)
\(R_{AB} = \dfrac{4 \times 4}{4 + 4} = 2\ \Omega\), \(R_{CD} = \dfrac{6 \times 6}{6 + 6} = 3\ \Omega\)
\(R_{BC} = 1\ \Omega\)
\(R_{T} = R_{eq} = 2 + 1 + 3 = 6\ \Omega\)
\(\therefore\) Equivalent Resistance is \(6\ \Omega\)
ii) Current in each resistor :
Total current \(I\) in the circuit is,
\(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R_{T} + r} = \dfrac{15}{6 + 1} = 2.1\) A
Consider resistors between A and B.
Let \(I_{1}\) be the current through one of the \(4\ \Omega\) resistors and \(I_{2}\) be the current in the other resistor
\(I_{1} \times 4 = I_{2} \times 4\)
that is, \(I_{1} = I_{2}\) from symmetry of the two arms.
But \(I_{1} + I_{2} = I = 2.1\) A
\(\therefore I_{1} = I_{2} = 1.05\) A
that is, the current in each \(4\ \Omega\) resistor is 1.05 A, the current in \(1\ \Omega\) resistor between B and C would be 2.1 A.
Now, consider the resistances between C and D
Let \(I_{3}\) be the current through one of the \(6\ \Omega\) resistors and \(I_{4}\) be the current in the other resistor.
\(I_{3} \times 6 = I_{4} \times 6\)
\(\therefore I_{3} = I_{4} = 1.05\) A
That is, current in each \(6\ \Omega\) resistor is 1.05 A
iii) Voltage drop across AB is \(V_{AB}\)
\(V_{AB} = I \times R_{AB} = 2.1 \times 2 = 4.2\) V
Voltage drop across BC is \(V_{BC}\)
\(V_{BC} = I \times R_{BC} = 2.1 \times 1 = 2.1\) V
Voltage drop across CD is \(V_{CD}\)
\(V_{CD} = I \times R_{CD} = 2.1 \times 3 = 6.3\) V
[Note : Total voltage drop across AD is (4.2 V + 2.1 V + 6.3 V) = 12.6 V, while its emf is 15 V. The loss of the voltage is 2.4 V].
